content: Parent education and training programs have been shown to enhance maternal psychosocial health, address child behavioral problems, and improve parenting practices. This review specifically evaluates the impact of parenting interventions on reducing unintentional injuries in children. The objective of this review was to determine the effectiveness of parenting interventions in preventing unintentional injuries in children aged 18 years or younger. Additionally, it aimed to assess whether these interventions increased the use and possession of safety equipment and improved safety practices among parents. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, BIOSIS Preview, PsycINFO, and others. Abstracts from relevant conferences and journals were also manually reviewed. The search was completed in January 2011. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled trials (non-RCTs), and controlled before-and-after studies (CBAs). Eligible studies evaluated parenting interventions targeting parents of children aged 18 years or younger and reported outcomes related to child injuries (unintentional or unspecified intent) or parental safety practices, such as the use of safety equipment or home safety assessments (e.g., the HOME scale). Parenting interventions were defined as structured programs with a specified protocol, manual, or curriculum designed to modify parental knowledge, attitudes, or skills across various parenting topics. Two authors independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed the quality of the included studies. Pooled relative risks (RRs) were calculated using random-effects models. The review included 22 studies: 16 RCTs, two non-RCTs, one partially randomized trial with two randomized intervention arms and one non-randomized control arm, two CBA studies, and one quasi-randomized controlled trial. Seventeen studies provided interventions that combined parenting education with additional support services, 15 of which were home-visiting programs, while two were based in pediatric practices. Two studies offered purely educational interventions. Most studies (19 out of 22) recruited families from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds, including single mothers, teenage mothers, first-time mothers, and mothers with learning difficulties. A meta-analysis of 10 RCTs involving 5,074 participants revealed that families receiving the intervention had a significantly lower risk of child injury compared to control families (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.94). Sensitivity analyses, which included only RCTs with a low risk of bias, confirmed the robustness of these findings. However, when analyses were restricted to studies with low risk of selection bias due to inadequate allocation concealment, the effect size was no longer statistically significant. Several studies reported fewer home hazards or an increased number of safety practices among intervention families. Of the 10 studies that assessed the HOME scale, data from three RCTs were included in a meta-analysis, which found no significant difference in the quality of the home environment between intervention and control groups (mean difference 0.57, 95% CI -0.59 to 1.72). Nevertheless, most studies that evaluated home safety practices, home hazards, or composite home safety scores reported statistically significant improvements favoring the intervention group. Using the GRADE framework, the overall quality of the evidence was rated as moderate. In conclusion, parenting interventions, particularly those delivered in the home and involving multi-faceted approaches, are effective in reducing child injuries. There is also consistent evidence suggesting that these interventions improve home safety. However, the evidence primarily pertains to families from disadvantaged populations who are at higher risk of adverse child health outcomes or who may benefit from additional support. Further research is needed to understand the mechanisms by which these interventions reduce injuries, identify the essential components of effective parenting interventions, and evaluate the applicability of these findings to other population groups.
